source.title: Finding the Minimal Parameter Budget for Implicit Reasoning: A Data Complexity Driven Scaling Law for Language Models
source.authors: Xinyi Wang; Shawn Tan; Shen-Bo Xu; Mingyu Jin; W. Wang; Rameswar Panda; Yikang Shen

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out test loss across model sizes in a knowledge-graph reasoning setting and reports non-monotonic, U-shaped curves, qualifying monotonic power-law scaling in that setting.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports reasoning accuracy, optimal model sizes, and a regression between optimal model size and graph search entropy. The loss curves in Figures 1 and 3 are plots without extractable per-model values in the supplied text. Results cited from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study pretrains Llama-architecture models (0.3M–1.3B) from scratch on knowledge-graph triples. It reports held-out triple-completion loss across model sizes: U-shaped under prolonged training, not monotonically falling. This is a new setting, a fixed small dataset trained for many epochs, that bears on whether the power-law form carries over (V5) and on curves bending away from a single power law (V7). Because data is fixed and is the bottleneck, V1's condition (other factors not the bottleneck) is not met, so V1 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors find non-monotonic test loss in model size for implicit knowledge-graph reasoning. With enough training, a smallest sufficient model reaches the best loss, and larger models can match it but may overfit. They state the U-shape arises only under prolonged training. They also report an approximately linear law between optimal size and graph search entropy (≈0.008 bits per parameter), and say results are not directly applicable to real text-corpus pretraining.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains Llama-architecture models from scratch on synthetic or real-world knowledge-graph triples and measures held-out triple-completion loss and reasoning accuracy. It does not reproduce the original studies' ordinary language-corpus loss sweeps or fixed-compute allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The clarity and reproducibility of the FB15K-237 trend vary with triple representation: random IDs give the clearest pattern, while the two natural-language representations are noisier. The smallest model attaining best achievable loss also changes with training duration before stabilizing.

fits_no_version.finding: The smallest model reaching best achievable held-out loss grows with graph complexity (triples, relations, entities) and is roughly linear in graph search entropy (R2=0.85). This holds on FB15K-237 too.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In knowledge-graph reasoning pretraining, the optimal (smallest sufficient) model size scales linearly with graph search entropy, about 124 parameters per bit.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The study is limited to simplified knowledge-graph pretraining, and the authors say its results do not directly apply to real-world language-model pretraining. The paper notes limited compute and time constrained the model sizes sampled and that experiments inspect step 10k rather than training indefinitely. Per-model loss values for the plotted sweeps are not extractable from the supplied text.

untested.parts: Not tested: no text-corpus pretraining, and data is fixed and repeated, so V1's 'others not bottleneck' condition fails. No token or compute sweeps.
No extrapolation of small-run fits to larger runs.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested. No power law is fitted to the knowledge-graph losses.
No downstream tasks or predictability from pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitted exponents or fitting methods. No compute-optimal split.

missing.what: Training loss decreases monotonically with model size while held-out loss is U-shaped. This distinguishes overfitting from a failure of fitting capacity.
Authors state fewer training steps give larger models much better performance, and that the U-shape arises only under prolonged training.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V1 'challenges' label is dropped. The U-shape occurs with a fixed, heavily repeated small dataset, the regime where Kaplan-style L(N,D) already predicts overfitting, so V1's condition is unmet. The evidence is reassigned to V5 (repeated-data, non-text regime) and V7 (bending curves). All loss values are figure-only, so the verdicts rest on the authors' verbal descriptions.

versions.untested_parts: Only model-size sweeps are relevant here; the study does not test ordinary language-corpus pretraining loss or scaling against tokens and compute.
No power law fitted on small runs is tested as a predictor of runs orders of magnitude larger.
The study does not compare parameter and token allocations at fixed compute or fit their growth against compute.
Architecture dimensions vary across model sizes, but the study does not compare architectures at a fixed parameter count.
No other modality, repeated-data regime, fine-tuning, or transfer setting is tested.
The study evaluates held-out knowledge-graph completion, not downstream-task performance or its predictability from pretraining loss.

The study shows non-monotonic curves and some sensitivity to data representation and training duration, but does not compare fitted exponents across fitting methods or test compute-optimal allocation trends.

relationships.condition: Knowledge-graph triple pretraining with a fixed dataset under prolonged training (many epochs), FB15K-237
relationships.reason: Held-out loss falls with size only up to an optimum, then rises (U-shape), so the monotone power-law form fails here (r1-r3). This is read from the authors' description; values are figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: Held-out loss decreased up to an optimal model size and then increased, producing a U-shaped curve rather than monotone power-law decay.

relationships.condition: FB15K-237 test loss versus model size across training-step counts and triple representations
relationships.reason: Curves bend away from a single power law into a U-shape. The shape depends on training duration and representation: random IDs are clean, natural-language versions noisy (r1-r3).
relationships.display_finding: Test loss becomes U-shaped rather than following a single power law, with clear curves for random identifiers and noisier curves for natural-language representations as training duration varies.
